title: Outbox, saga, CDC and workflows
scopeHtml: Scope: dual writes, transactional outbox, CDC, sagas and durable workflows.

notes.title: The dual-write problem
notes.html:
Updating your database and publishing an event are two separate systems, and you cannot make both succeed atomically with a simple code sequence.

db.save(order)          # step 1 succeeds
kafka.send(order_event) # step 2 fails (broker down) -> event lost

Reverse the order and a crash after the publish leaves an event for an order that was never saved. A distributed transaction (2PC/XA) across DB and broker is slow and unsupported by most brokers.

Worked example. At 1,000 orders/s with 99.99% broker availability per call, you lose about 0.1 events/s, or around 8,640 orders per day with no downstream notification (no inventory reservation, no email). Small percentage, big absolute number.

Industry examples. This is the reason Debezium, Uber's and Shopify's outbox pipelines, and the "Transactional Outbox" pattern (Chris Richardson, microservices.io) exist.

Everyday analogy. Signing a contract and mailing a copy: if you sign but the post office is closed, the other party never learns of the deal.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "just retry the publish". If the process dies, no one retries.
  • Proposing 2PC across Kafka and a DB as a casual solution.

notes.title: Transactional outbox
notes.html:
Write the business row and an "outbox" row in the SAME database transaction. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes to the broker. Atomicity comes from the local DB; publishing becomes at-least-once.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders(id, user_id, total) VALUES (42, 7, 999);
INSERT INTO outbox(id, aggregate_id, type, payload, created_at)
VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), 42, 'OrderPlaced', '{"orderId":42,"total":999}', now());
COMMIT;

Relay options:

  • Polling publisher: SELECT ... FROM outbox WHERE published=false ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED every 100 ms, publish, mark/delete. Simple; adds DB load and latency (about the poll interval).
  • CDC (log tailing): Debezium reads the WAL/binlog (see next section). Lower latency, no polling.

The relay can crash after publishing and before marking, so events can duplicate: consumers must be idempotent (carry the outbox id as the dedup key; see the delivery notes). Clean the table periodically (delete after 7 days) to keep it small.

Gravity. Outbox is the pragmatic default: cheap, uses what you have, reversible. Alternatives: event sourcing (heavier model change), 2PC (rarely sensible). It breaks when the outbox table becomes a hot spot at very high write rates (consider partitioning by time, or CDC).

Industry examples. Debezium's outbox event router; widely used at companies on Kafka plus Postgres/MySQL. AWS offers DynamoDB Streams, which gives a similar guarantee.

Everyday analogy. Writing "to post tomorrow" on the same page as the letter you filed; a clerk later mails whatever is on the list.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that the outbox gives at-least-once, not exactly-once.
  • Publishing directly from the request thread "as well", reintroducing dual writes.
  • Ordering: concurrent transactions may commit out of id order; key events per aggregate.

notes.title: Change data capture (CDC)
notes.html:
CDC turns a database's commit log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog, Mongo oplog) into a stream of row-level change events. Tools like Debezium read the log with minimal load on the DB and publish to Kafka, one topic per table.

Uses:

  • Outbox relay without polling.
  • Keep search (Elasticsearch) and cache in sync.
  • Feed a data warehouse; replicate between systems; strangler-fig migration off a legacy DB.
  • Invalidate Redis keys when the row changes.

Config highlights (Postgres): wal_level=logical, a replication slot per connector. Monitor slot lag: an abandoned replication slot makes Postgres retain WAL and can fill the disk. Initial snapshot, then streaming; schema changes need care (Schema Registry).

Worked example. Orders table updates 2,000 rows/s. Debezium emits 2,000 events/s at about 1 KB (2 MB/s). Elasticsearch indexer consumes in batches of 500 and lags under 2 s.

Alternatives. Trigger-based CDC (slower, intrusive), timestamp polling (misses deletes and rapid changes), dual writes (unsafe). Log-based is the robust one.

Industry examples. Debezium at many companies; LinkedIn's Databus; Facebook's invalidation daemon on the MySQL binlog; AWS DMS; Netflix DBLog.

Everyday analogy. Reading the accountant's journal to know every change, rather than asking for the full ledger over and over.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring replication slot lag and WAL disk growth.
  • Assuming CDC events have business meaning; they are row changes, often leaking your table schema to other teams.
  • Transaction boundaries across tables are not automatically preserved in consumers.

notes.title: Sagas for distributed transactions
notes.html:
A saga is a sequence of local transactions across services, where each step has a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. It replaces one big ACID transaction with eventual consistency.

Example: place order. 1) Create order (PENDING). 2) Reserve inventory. 3) Charge payment. 4) Confirm order. If payment fails: release inventory (compensation), cancel the order.

Two coordination styles:

  • Choreography: services react to each other's events. No central brain; simple for 2 to 3 steps, hard to follow when large.
  • Orchestration: a coordinator (saga orchestrator or workflow engine) tells each service what to do and handles failures. Clearer, easier to monitor, an additional component.

Rules: each step and each compensation must be idempotent and retryable; compensations are "semantic undo" (refund, not delete); isolation is weak (others can see intermediate state), so use states like PENDING and handle with care.

Worked example. Flight + hotel + car booking. Car fails after flight and hotel are booked: compensation cancels hotel then flight (fees may apply, so compensations are business operations, not rollbacks). Timeline per saga about 2 s with 3 steps; orchestrator persists its state after each step to survive crashes.

Gravity. Choose sagas only when data truly lives in different services. If you can keep related data in one database, a local ACID transaction is better. Moving between choreography and orchestration is a heavy refactor.

Industry examples. Uber Cadence (now Temporal) for trip and payment flows, Netflix Conductor, AWS Step Functions, Camunda, and Axon framework.

Everyday analogy. Planning a holiday: if the hotel can't be booked, you cancel the flight you already booked (and may pay a fee).

Common interview traps.

  • Compensations that can themselves fail with no retry plan.
  • Non-idempotent steps.
  • Forgetting timeouts: a step that never answers needs a deadline.
  • Claiming sagas are ACID; they lack isolation.

notes.title: Durable workflows
notes.html:
A workflow engine runs long, multi-step business processes with its state saved durably, so it survives crashes, deploys and week-long waits. You write the flow as normal code; the engine persists each step, retries, timers and signals.

Temporal-style idea:

@WorkflowMethod
public void placeOrder(Order o) {
  inventory.reserve(o);                   // activity, retried automatically
  try {
    payment.charge(o);                    // activity
  } catch (ActivityFailure e) {
    inventory.release(o);                 // compensation
    throw e;
  }
  Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofDays(7));     // durable timer, survives restarts
  email.sendReviewRequest(o);
}

Engine records an event history; after a crash the code is replayed deterministically to rebuild state, skipping activities already done. So workflow code must be deterministic (no random or wall-clock inside; use the workflow APIs), and activities must be idempotent because they have at-least-once execution.

When to use. Order fulfilment, onboarding, payouts, KYC, subscriptions with timers. When not to: simple fire-and-forget jobs (use a queue), or sub-10-ms flows.

Alternatives. Hand-rolled state machine in a DB plus queue (works for small flows, grows messy); Step Functions (managed, JSON/ASL, per-transition cost).

Industry examples. Uber (Cadence), Stripe, Netflix, Snap, Coinbase (Temporal); AWS Step Functions; Airflow for batch DAGs (different purpose).

Everyday analogy. A to-do list in a notebook that survives anything: if you pass out, a colleague picks up from the last ticked item.

Common interview traps.

  • Non-deterministic code in the workflow body.
  • Treating the workflow engine as a database for large payloads; keep payloads small, use references.
  • Skipping idempotency in activities.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Dual writes (DB plus broker) are unsafe: a crash between them loses or invents events.
  • Transactional outbox: business row plus outbox row in one transaction; a relay publishes at-least-once; consumers dedup by outbox id.
  • CDC (Debezium on WAL/binlog) is the best relay and also syncs search, caches and warehouses; watch replication slot lag.
  • Sagas replace distributed transactions with local transactions plus compensations; choreography for small flows, orchestration for clarity; steps must be idempotent.
  • Durable workflow engines (Temporal, Step Functions) persist state, retry, and handle timers; keep code deterministic and activities idempotent.

questions.promptHtml: What is the dual-write problem, and why can't you just retry the publish?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the entry point to outbox, CDC and sagas; weak answers reveal shallow event-driven experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Saving to the database and publishing to a broker are two separate systems with no shared transaction, so one can succeed while the other fails. If the DB write succeeds and the publish fails, downstream never hears about the order; reverse the order and a crash leaves an event for data that was never saved. Retrying in the same process does not help if the process dies, because nobody remembers to retry.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
db.save(order)           # step 1 succeeds
kafka.send(order_event)  # step 2 fails (broker down) -> event lost

Scale makes it concrete: at 1,000 orders/s and 99.99% availability per publish you lose about 0.1 event/s, about 8,640 orders per day with no inventory reservation or email. A 2PC/XA transaction across DB and broker is slow and unsupported by most brokers. The fix is to make one atomic local write and derive the other asynchronously: the transactional outbox.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Just retry the publish."
  • Casually proposing 2PC across Kafka and a DB.
  • Publishing inside the DB transaction before commit (event for a rolled-back row).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which order is "less bad"? -> Neither; DB-first loses events, publish-first creates phantom events.
  2. Why not XA? -> Latency, locks held, brokers rarely support it, and coordinator failure complexity.
  3. What is the clean solution? -> Outbox row in the same local transaction plus a relay or CDC.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "wrap in try/catch and retry". Senior: names the atomicity gap, quantifies loss and proposes outbox/CDC.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Missing "order placed" events caused warehouse backlogs that were only discovered by a daily reconciliation.

questions.promptHtml: How does the transactional outbox pattern work, what delivery guarantee does it give, and what are its limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know both the mechanism and that it is at-least-once, not exactly-once.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I write the business row and an outbox row in the same local DB transaction, so they commit or roll back together. A separate relay (a polling publisher or CDC) reads the outbox and publishes to the broker. Publishing is at-least-once because the relay may crash after publishing and before marking the row, so consumers must dedup using the outbox id.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders(id, user_id, total) VALUES (42, 7, 999);
INSERT INTO outbox(id, aggregate_id, type, payload, created_at)
VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), 42, 'OrderPlaced', '{"orderId":42,"total":999}', now());
COMMIT;

Polling relay: SELECT ... FROM outbox WHERE published=false ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED every 100 ms, publish, mark or delete. Simple, adds DB load and latency of about the poll interval. CDC relay: Debezium reads the WAL/binlog, lower latency, no polling. Clean the table (delete after 7 days). Limits: a hot outbox table at very high write rates; ordering across concurrent transactions (key events per aggregate).

Service -> (orders + outbox, one tx) -> Relay -> Kafka -> Consumers (dedup by outbox id)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling it exactly-once.
  • Also publishing directly from the request thread (reintroduces dual writes).
  • Never cleaning the outbox.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why SKIP LOCKED? -> Several relays can poll without blocking each other.
  2. How do you preserve per-aggregate order? -> Key by aggregate id; single relay per partition range; sequence numbers.
  3. When is outbox the wrong tool? -> Extreme write rates where the outbox table becomes the bottleneck; consider CDC on the main tables or event sourcing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "write both in a transaction". Senior: relay options, at-least-once consequence, ordering and table hygiene.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An outbox with no cleanup grew to 400 GB and made the polling query scan for minutes.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout service occasionally has orders in the DB with no OrderPlaced event, so inventory is never reserved. Broker was healthy during most failures; a few coincided with pod restarts.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(Order o) {
  orderRepo.save(o);
  kafka.send("orders", o.id(), toEvent(o));   // fire-and-forget
}
@Transactional
fun placeOrder(o: Order) {
  orderRepo.save(o)
  kafka.send("orders", o.id, toEvent(o))      // fire-and-forget
}
questions.promptHtml: What are the bugs and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add acks=all and retries" or "move the send after the transaction".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What DB and broker? Is there a CDC tool available? Are consumers idempotent? What is acceptable event latency?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run a reconciliation query for orders without events and republish them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pod killed after the DB commit and before the send completes (async buffer lost); (b) send inside the transaction can publish before commit, so a rollback leaves a phantom event; (c) broker blips (secondary).
  4. How I'd verify: Compare order ids to event ids over a day; check shutdown logs for unflushed producer.
  5. Root cause: Two systems, no atomicity; fire-and-forget hides failures.
  6. Fix: Insert an outbox row in the same transaction, relay it with Debezium or a polling publisher, make consumers dedup by event id.
  7. Prevention: A daily reconciliation metric (orders minus events), and a lint rule against kafka.send in transactional services.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not 2PC; not "send after commit with retries" as the only protection, since a crash still loses it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Latency requirement 50 ms? -> CDC relay, not 1 s polling.
  • Why not event sourcing? -> A heavier model change; outbox is the pragmatic default.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a rolling deploy killed pods every night and each one lost a few in-flight events.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes acks only.
  • Hire: outbox with relay.
  • Strong hire: also names phantom events, reconciliation and dedup at consumers.

questions.promptHtml: What is change data capture, how does Debezium do it, and what operational risks does it carry?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: CDC appears in outbox, search sync and migration answers; operational awareness marks seniority.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CDC turns the database's commit log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog) into a stream of row-change events, with low load on the DB. Debezium reads the log, publishes one topic per table to Kafka, and downstream consumers keep search, caches or a warehouse in sync or act as the outbox relay. The main risk is an abandoned replication slot, which makes Postgres retain WAL until the disk fills.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Postgres needs wal_level=logical and a replication slot per connector; Debezium takes an initial snapshot, then streams. Alternatives are weaker: triggers are intrusive and slower, timestamp polling misses deletes and rapid changes, dual writes are unsafe. Example: 2,000 row updates/s at about 1 KB is 2 MB/s of events. Caveats: events are row changes that leak your table schema; transaction boundaries across tables are not automatically preserved for consumers; schema changes need a Schema Registry and compatibility rules.

(Postgres WAL) -> Debezium -> Kafka -> Search indexer / Cache invalidator / Warehouse

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring slot lag and WAL disk growth.
  • Treating row events as business events.
  • Forgetting deletes and schema evolution.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens when the connector is down for a day? -> Postgres retains WAL for the slot; disk grows; alert on slot lag.
  2. How do you avoid leaking the schema? -> Use an outbox table with a business payload instead of raw table events.
  3. Initial load of a 2 TB table? -> Snapshot with care (incremental snapshots), watch load and time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it streams DB changes". Senior: slot lag risk, schema coupling, alternatives and snapshot cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A forgotten test connector's slot retained 600 GB of WAL and took a primary out of disk space.

questions.contextHtml:
A polling outbox relay (single instance, 100 ms poll, batch 100) works at 300 events/s. Marketing plans a 10x event; expected 3,000/s. Metrics at 300/s:

relay: 3 polls/s x 100 = max 300 events/s  (batch-bound)
outbox backlog: 0
DB CPU due to polling: 8%

At 1,000/s in a load test the backlog grows by 700/s.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Poll faster" or add a second relay without handling duplicates and order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is ordering required per aggregate? End-to-end latency SLO? Can I move to CDC? How long is the peak?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise batch size to 1,000 and loop without sleeping while the backlog is non-empty; ceiling becomes about 10 polls/s x 1,000 = 10,000/s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The cap is batch x poll rate, not DB capacity (red herring: DB CPU is fine).
  4. How I'd verify: Load test with larger batches and measure p99 latency and DB load.
  5. Root cause: Throughput ceiling = batch size x polls per second.
  6. Fix: Short term: bigger batches and an adaptive poll (no sleep when full). Long term: several relays using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED sharded by hash(aggregate_id) % N to keep per-aggregate order; or Debezium CDC for no polling.
  7. Prevention: Alert on outbox age (oldest unpublished row) and backlog size.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not unsharded multiple relays (reorder events for an aggregate); consumers still dedup by outbox id.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Relay crashes after publish before mark? -> Duplicates; dedup at the consumer.
  • Table growth at 3,000/s x 1 KB? -> 3 MB/s, about 260 GB/day; delete published rows in batches or partition by day.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: backlog hid behind "all green" dashboards because only relay errors were monitored, not outbox age.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: poll faster.
  • Hire: batch math and multiple relays.
  • Strong hire: sharding for order, cleanup, age alert and CDC alternative.

questions.contextHtml: Order flow: Order, Inventory, Payment, Shipping, Notification services. Currently choreographed with events. Problems: nobody can answer "where is order 8812?"; adding a fraud check needed changes in 3 services; failures leave stuck PENDING orders (about 0.3% = 150/day at 50k orders/day).
questions.promptHtml: Would you change the coordination style, and how do you handle failure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Orchestration is always better" or "keep choreography, add logging".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many steps and teams? Are flows long-lived with timers? Do we have a workflow engine already? What is the stuck-order cost?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A reaper job: orders PENDING over N minutes trigger compensation and an alert.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Lost or unhandled events, missing timeouts, no central state.
  4. How I'd verify: Trace a stuck order across services (correlation id), count by last-seen step.
  5. Root cause: No owner of the end-to-end state or deadlines; flow knowledge is scattered across five services.
  6. Fix: Orchestrate with a saga orchestrator/workflow engine for this 5-step flow: persist state per step, retries, timeouts, compensations (release inventory, refund, cancel). Steps and compensations idempotent; explicit PENDING/CONFIRMED/CANCELLED states.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard of in-flight sagas by state and age; alerts on stuck sagas.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Orchestration adds a component and coupling to the orchestrator; I would keep choreography for simple 2-3 step flows. Switching styles later is a heavy refactor.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Orchestrator goes down? -> State is durable; it resumes; run it highly available.
  • Compensation fails? -> Retry with backoff, then alert a human.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: 150 stuck orders a day were "normal" until a team added a single overdue-order metric.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: dogmatic.
  • Hire: chooses orchestration with compensations.
  • Strong hire: timeouts, idempotency, observability and the trade-off of the extra component.

questions.promptHtml: How does a durable workflow engine (Temporal or Step Functions style) survive crashes and week-long waits, and what rules must your code follow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of event-history replay, determinism and activity idempotency, which are the usual pitfalls.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The engine records every step in an event history. After a crash or a deploy it replays the workflow code deterministically against that history to rebuild state, skipping activities already completed. So workflow code must be deterministic (no random, wall clock or direct I/O; use the workflow APIs), and activities have at-least-once execution, so they must be idempotent. Timers are durable, so a 7-day sleep survives restarts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
@WorkflowMethod
public void placeOrder(Order o) {
  inventory.reserve(o);                 // activity, retried automatically
  try { payment.charge(o); }            // activity
  catch (ActivityFailure e) { inventory.release(o); throw e; } // compensation
  Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofDays(7));   // durable timer
  email.sendReviewRequest(o);
}

Use for order fulfilment, onboarding, payouts, KYC, subscriptions with timers. Do not use for simple fire-and-forget jobs (a queue) or sub-10 ms flows. Keep payloads small and pass references; the history is not a database. A hand-rolled state machine in a DB plus a queue works for small flows, Step Functions is managed with per-transition cost.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Non-deterministic code in the workflow body.
  • Big payloads in history.
  • Non-idempotent activities.
  • Changing workflow code without versioning while executions are in flight.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you deploy a code change safely? -> Versioning/patch APIs so replays of old histories still match.
  2. Why are activities at-least-once? -> The worker may crash after the effect before reporting completion.
  3. Saga vs workflow? -> A saga is the pattern; the engine provides durability, retries and timers to implement it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it retries steps". Senior: replay model, determinism, versioning, idempotency and when not to use it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deploy changed the step order of a workflow and thousands of in-flight executions failed replay.

questions.contextHtml:
Sunday 04:10 pager: primary Postgres disk at 94% (2 TB volume). Application traffic is normal. Findings:

SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn))
FROM pg_replication_slots;

 slot_name          | active | retained
 debezium_orders    | f      | 1.4 TB
 old_analytics_test | f      | 220 GB

The Debezium connector crashed Friday evening after a schema change; nobody was paged because Kafka lag alerts looked fine (no new messages).
questions.promptHtml: What do you do in the next hour, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Deletes WAL files manually, or just expands the disk and goes back to sleep.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the debezium slot needed (can we resnapshot)? Is anyone using the test slot? How fast does disk grow now? Are there physical replicas that depend on WAL?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop old_analytics_test (pg_drop_replication_slot) immediately; that frees 220 GB; expand the volume if growth is imminent.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) inactive slots pin WAL; (b) a long-running transaction; (c) archiving failure. (a) is confirmed by active = f.
  4. How I'd verify: The query above, pg_stat_replication, disk growth rate, connector logs for the crash cause.
  5. Root cause: An inactive logical slot forces Postgres to retain all WAL since restart_lsn; the connector crashed and monitoring watched Kafka (silent) rather than the slot.
  6. Fix: Short term: fix the connector (schema change handling) and let it catch up and release WAL (1.4 TB may take hours; watch disk); if the disk would fill first, drop the slot and re-snapshot, accepting the resync cost and a gap that the snapshot covers. Long term: max_slot_wal_keep_size (verify version support) as a safety cap, accept slot invalidation over primary outage.
  7. Prevention: Alert on slot retained bytes and active=false for over 10 minutes; connector health checks; schema-change runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Never delete WAL files by hand (corruption). Dropping a slot loses the stream position, so consumers need a resnapshot.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why no alert? -> "No messages" looks like healthy lag; alert on the source side.
  • Could this happen with MySQL? -> Different: binlog retention expires; connector may lose position.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a forgotten dev slot filled a production primary three weeks after the experiment ended.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes WAL files.
  • Hire: identifies slots and drops/fixes them.
  • Strong hire: decides drop-vs-recover with data, adds retention cap and slot alerting.

questions.contextHtml:
A travel saga: book flight, book hotel, book car. The car service was down 20 minutes. The orchestrator compensated hotel then flight, but the flight cancellation endpoint timed out; the orchestrator logged the error and marked the saga FAILED. Customers kept flight tickets they were never charged for in the final state, while the airline charged cancellation fees on a different subset. Support got 300 tickets.

saga 77a1: bookFlight OK, bookHotel OK, bookCar FAIL
          cancelHotel OK, cancelFlight TIMEOUT -> state=FAILED (no retry)
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with the saga design and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the timeout" or "use a distributed transaction".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is cancelFlight idempotent (what happens on a retry after a timeout that actually succeeded)? What fees apply? Is there an owner for stuck sagas?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Query all sagas in FAILED with an incomplete compensation; retry cancelFlight using the booking id as the idempotency key; contact customers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Compensation treated as best-effort; timeout equals unknown result; no terminal state like COMPENSATION_PENDING.
  4. How I'd verify: Reconcile saga records against provider bookings.
  5. Root cause: Compensations can fail too, and the design had no retry and no human escalation path; a timeout does not mean "did not happen".
  6. Fix: Compensations are retried with backoff until success (bounded, then manual queue); both steps and compensations idempotent; persist per-step state; states: RUNNING, COMPENSATING, COMPENSATED, STUCK (alert). Reorder risk: put the most failure-prone or non-refundable step last, or use reservation/hold semantics (book with TTL, confirm at the end).
  7. Prevention: Chaos test dependencies; alert on sagas in COMPENSATING over N minutes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not 2PC across external airlines (impossible); accept that compensations are business operations with possible fees.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Saga isolation anomalies? -> Others can see intermediate state; use PENDING status and semantic locks.
  • Airline API non-idempotent? -> Lookup by reference before retry.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a saga marked FAILED after a single compensation timeout left a quiet trail of orphan bookings for a month.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer timeout/2PC.
  • Hire: retried idempotent compensations.
  • Strong hire: explicit states, hold-and-confirm design, step ordering and alerts.

questions.contextHtml:
A Temporal-style OnboardingWorkflow has 40,000 in-flight executions (many waiting on a 3-day timer). A deploy inserts a new activity runFraudCheck() between createAccount and sendWelcome, and replaces a UUID.randomUUID() call with System.currentTimeMillis(). After deploy:

ERROR WorkflowTaskFailure: NonDeterministicException:
  history event 7 ActivityTaskScheduled(sendWelcome) != command ScheduleActivity(runFraudCheck)
tasks failing: 38,900, workflow stuck, retried every 10 s
questions.promptHtml: Mitigate and explain how to deploy such changes properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll forward and restart", unaware of why replay fails.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I roll back the code quickly? Are histories intact? Is the new activity required for old executions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the worker deployment to the old code; executions resume replaying fine (stuck workflow tasks just retry; the state is safe in history).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Changed command sequence breaks replay; non-deterministic API (currentTimeMillis, random) produces different values on replay; a serializer change (secondary).
  4. How I'd verify: The exception text pointing to the event mismatch; replay tests against exported histories.
  5. Root cause: On replay the engine re-executes the code and matches commands to history; inserting a step or changing deterministic inputs breaks the match.
  6. Fix: Use the engine's versioning/patching API (Workflow.getVersion or patched) so old executions follow the old path and new ones the new; use Workflow.randomUUID() and Workflow.currentTimeMillis(); run replay tests on captured production histories in CI.
  7. Prevention: Replay-test gate in CI, canary workers, an internal rule: no I/O, random or time outside workflow APIs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not terminating the 40,000 executions to "start fresh" (customers stranded); keep old branches until all old executions finish, then clean up.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Long-lived workflow with years of versions? -> Continue-as-new and a versioning policy.
  • Can activities change freely? -> Their implementation yes (still idempotent); their scheduling order no.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: one deploy stalled every in-flight onboarding for an hour; rollback saved the day and replay tests became mandatory.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts.
  • Hire: rolls back and explains determinism.
  • Strong hire: versioning API, replay tests in CI and caution on terminations.

questions.contextHtml: A monolith writes orders to MySQL and calls kafka.send afterwards (dual write). Reconciliation shows 0.05% of 400,000 daily orders (200) lack events. You must adopt the outbox with zero downtime and no duplicated downstream effects. Consumers are not all idempotent yet; 12 teams consume orders.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Replace the code in one release and hope.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which consumers are non-idempotent and who owns them? Is Debezium available for MySQL binlog? Event schema stability? Rollback needs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a reconciliation job that republishes missing events (consumers must dedup) as an interim.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: duplicate events during overlap; order changes; schema differences between direct and outbox events.
  4. How I'd verify: Shadow-compare outbox events with direct events by id for a week.
  5. Root cause (of the plan's concerns): Moving the publish point while consumers assume at-most-once-per-id.
  6. Fix (plan): Step 1: add an outbox table and write rows in the same transaction, relay disabled (shadow). Step 2: make the event id deterministic (orderId:eventType:version) so the old and new path produce the same id. Step 3: ask all 12 consumers to dedup by that id, tracking a checklist. Step 4: enable the relay to a shadow topic and diff against the live topic. Step 5: cut the relay over to the real topic and remove the direct send, behind a flag with instant rollback. Step 6: delete rows after retention.
  7. Prevention: Consumer idempotency as an onboarding requirement; contract tests; outbox age alert.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a big-bang switch; not requiring all consumers before shadowing, but I would not cut over until the money-handling consumers are idempotent.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why a deterministic id? -> So a duplicate from both paths during overlap collapses at dedup.
  • Rollback? -> Flip the flag back; outbox rows are harmless.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a one-shot cutover double-published a day of orders because one consumer was not idempotent.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang.
  • Hire: shadow, diff and flagged cutover.
  • Strong hire: deterministic ids, consumer readiness checklist, rollback and retention.

questions.contextHtml:
Outbox at 20,000 events/s with 4 relay instances (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, batch 500). Consumers report that for some orders OrderShipped arrives before OrderPaid. Outbox ids are auto-increment. Another team insists "ids are monotonic so order is guaranteed". Observed:

tx A (paid)    : outbox id 9,001 inserted at 10:00:00.001, commits 10:00:00.250
tx B (shipped) : outbox id 9,002 inserted at 10:00:00.010, commits 10:00:00.040
relay 1 reads at 10:00:00.100: sees id 9,002 (committed), not 9,001 (not yet)
questions.promptHtml: Explain, fix, and say what ordering you can actually promise.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use one relay" or "sort by id", missing commit-order gaps.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the two events belong to one aggregate? Must consumers be strictly ordered or just never see Shipped before Paid? Can events carry sequence numbers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Consumers tolerate reordering by checking aggregate state/version and parking early events.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ids are allocated at insert, visibility at commit: higher id can be visible first; (b) multiple relays race (secondary); (c) Kafka partitioning by random key (check).
  4. How I'd verify: Compare commit timestamps and ids; check the producer key.
  5. Root cause: Sequence values are not commit-ordered; a relay that has passed id 9,002 may never re-read 9,001 if it tracks a high-water mark, or two relays interleave.
  6. Fix: Key events by aggregate id so one partition holds all of an order's events; use an aggregate version/sequence number assigned inside the transaction (optimistic lock on the aggregate row) and have consumers enforce expected_version; relays shard by hash(aggregate_id) so one aggregate is handled by one relay; or read via WAL (Debezium), which follows commit order.
  7. Prevention: Ordering tests under concurrency; consumer-side version checks and metrics for out-of-order arrivals.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Global ordering is unnecessary and expensive; I would promise per-aggregate order only. Not a single relay for all events at 20k/s.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two aggregates must be ordered (payment then shipment across services)? -> Use a saga/orchestrator, not outbox ordering.
  • Polling with a high-water mark? -> Use a lag window or process by aggregate to avoid skipping uncommitted ids.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: "ids are monotonic" survived every test and failed only under production concurrency.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes id order is commit order.
  • Hire: explains the gap and keys by aggregate.
  • Strong hire: versions, relay sharding or WAL-based reading, and a scoped ordering promise.
